Hangul is the Korean alphabet. Each syllable is a block. A vowel alone is written with **ㅇ** in front, which is silent at the start: 아 is just “a”.
아 · 어 · 오 · 우 · 으 · 이 (a · eo · o · u · eu · i)
Put a consonant in front of a vowel to make a syllable block: **ㄱ + ㅏ = 가** (ga). Read the block from left to right.
가 · 나 · 다 · 마 · 바 · 사 · 하 (ga · na · da · ma · ba · sa · ha)
Join syllable blocks to make words. Read each block, then say them together.
Adding a short stroke makes a **y**-sound: ㅏ → ㅑ (ya), ㅓ → ㅕ (yeo), ㅗ → ㅛ (yo), ㅜ → ㅠ (yu). ㅐ (ae) and ㅔ (e) sound very similar in modern Korean.
야 · 여 · 요 · 유 (ya · yeo · yo · yu)
ㄹ is between “r” and “l”. ㅈ (j), ㅊ (ch, with a puff of air), ㅋ (k, with a puff of air), ㅌ (t, with a puff of air) and ㅍ (p, with a puff of air) complete the basic consonants.
라 · 자 · 차 · 카 · 타 · 파 (ra · ja · cha · ka · ta · pa)
ㄲ, ㄸ, ㅃ, ㅆ and ㅉ are tense sounds: say them with a tight throat and no puff of air, like the first sound in “skate”.
까 · 따 · 빠 · 싸 · 짜 (kka · tta · ppa · ssa · jja)
A consonant under the syllable is called **받침 (batchim)**. It closes the syllable: 안 (an), 말 (mal), 밤 (bam), 강 (gang), 집 (jip), 책 (chaek). Only seven sounds are possible at the end: ㄱ ㄴ ㄷ ㄹ ㅁ ㅂ ㅇ.
안 · 말 · 밤 · 강 · 집 (an · mal · bam · gang · jip)
Read each word syllable by syllable. 학교 is read “hakgyo”: the final ㄱ of 학 is closed and the next syllable is pronounced tightly.
People and nature: 사람 (person), 나라 (country), 하늘 (sky), 산 (mountain), 강 (river), 꽃 (flower).
Polite greetings end in **-요** or **-니다**. 안녕하세요 works any time of day.
Short polite answers you can use every day. Korean adds **요** at the end to be polite.
When you meet someone new, say 만나서 반갑습니다. There are two ways to say goodbye: one for the person leaving, one for the person staying.
만나서 반갑습니다. (mannaseo bangapseumnida.) = Nice to meet you.
Use 실례합니다 to get someone's attention or pass by, 고마워요 to thank someone in a friendly way, 천만에요 to answer thanks, and 축하해요 to congratulate.
실례합니다. (sillyehamnida.) = Excuse me. / 고마워요. (gomawoyo.) = Thank you. (friendly)
Ask a name with 이름이 뭐예요? and a country with 어느 나라 사람이에요? Answer with 제 이름은 ___예요 or 저는 ___ 사람이에요.
이름이 뭐예요? (ireumi mwoyeyo?) = What is your name?
Among friends you can say 잘 가요 (goodbye), 내일 봐요 (see you tomorrow), 또 만나요 (see you again) and 잘 자요 (sleep well).
잘 가요. (jal gayo.) = Goodbye. (friendly) / 내일 봐요. (naeil bwayo.) = See you tomorrow.
Ask 잘 지냈어요? (Have you been well?) and answer 잘 지내요 (I'm doing well). 좋은 아침이에요 means “It's a good morning.”
잘 지내요. (jal jinaeyo.) = I'm doing well.
Say 도와주세요 to ask for help, 모르겠어요 when you do not know, 알겠어요 when you understand, and 다시 말해 주세요 to ask someone to say it again.
도와주세요. (dowajuseyo.) = Please help me. / 알겠어요. (algesseoyo.) = I understand.
좋아요 means good or fine, 싫어요 means you don't like it, 맞아요 means “that's right” and 틀려요 means “that's wrong”.
좋아요. (joayo.) = It's good. / 싫어요. (sireoyo.) = I don't like it.
Short signs are everywhere in Korea. **입구** is the entrance, **출구** the exit and **화장실** the restroom. On doors, **미세요** means push and **당기세요** means pull.
Before a meal say **잘 먹겠습니다**, and when you finish say **잘 먹었습니다**. A host welcomes you with **어서 오세요**, and **맛있어요** praises the food.
잘 먹겠습니다. (jal meokgetseumnida.) = Said before eating: “I will eat well.” / 잘 먹었습니다. (jal meogeotseumnida.) = Said after eating: “I ate well.”
**저는** means “I” (polite). Put **이에요** after a consonant and **예요** after a vowel to say “I am …”.
저는 학생이에요. (jeoneun haksaengieyo.) = I am a student.
Family words are used a lot in Korean, even for people who are not family.
Korean has two number systems: native Korean (하나, 둘, 셋 …) for counting things, and Sino-Korean (일, 이, 삼 …) for money, dates and minutes.
Continue the native Korean numbers: 여섯 (6), 일곱 (7), 여덟 (8), 아홉 (9), 열 (10).
여섯 · 일곱 · 여덟 · 아홉 · 열 (yeoseot · ilgop · yeodeol · ahop · yeol)
Sino-Korean numbers: 일 (1), 이 (2), 삼 (3), 사 (4), 오 (5), 육 (6), 칠 (7), 팔 (8), 구 (9), 십 (10). They are used for money, dates, phone numbers and minutes.
일 · 이 · 삼 · 사 · 오 · 육 · 칠 · 팔 · 구 · 십 (il · i · sam · sa · o · yuk · chil · pal · gu · sip)
Ask 몇 살이에요? (How old are you?). Ages use native numbers plus 살: 열 살 (10 years old), 스무 살 (20), 서른 살 (30).
몇 살이에요? (myeot sarieyo?) = How old are you?
Siblings use different words depending on who is speaking: a woman says 오빠 (older brother) and 언니 (older sister). Also 아들 (son), 딸 (daughter), 부모님 (parents).
오빠 (oppa) = older brother (said by a woman) / 언니 (eonni) = older sister (said by a woman)
Koreans often say 우리 (we, our) instead of “my”: 우리 가족 means “my family”. Count people with 명: 네 명 (four people).
Text messages use short polite sentences ending in **-요**. **지금 어디예요?** asks where you are, **곧 가요** means “I’m coming soon” and **늦어요** means “I’m late”.
지금 어디예요? (jigeum eodiyeyo?) = Where are you now? / 곧 가요. (got gayo.) = I’m coming soon.

When a syllable ends in a consonant and the next one starts with a vowel, the sound moves over: 책이 is read **chaegi** and 밥을 is read **babeul**. Some sounds also change their neighbours: 국물 is read **gungmul** and 같이 is read **gachi**.
Polite present-tense verbs end in **-아요 / -어요 / -해요**. The same form is used for “I”, “you” and “they”.
Put **에** after a place to say where you go or come: 학교에 가요. The verb comes last.
학교에 가요. (hakgyoe gayo.) = I go to school.
The object of a verb gets **을** after a consonant and **를** after a vowel: 밥을 먹어요, 커피를 마셔요.
밥을 먹어요. (babeul meogeoyo.) = I eat a meal.
밥 (rice, a meal), 빵 (bread), 과일 (fruit), 고기 (meat), 물 (water), 우유 (milk).
Say what you like with -를/을 좋아해요 and what you don't like with -를/을 싫어해요: 저는 사과를 좋아해요.
Describing words also end in -요: 커요 (big), 작아요 (small), 많아요 (many), 맛있어요 (delicious), 예뻐요 (pretty).
커요. (keoyo.) = It's big. / 작아요. (jagayo.) = It's small.
날씨 (weather), 더워요 (it's hot), 추워요 (it's cold), 비가 와요 (it's raining), 눈이 와요 (it's snowing).
더워요. (deowoyo.) = It's hot. / 추워요. (chuwoyo.) = It's cold.
Put **안** before a verb to say you don't do something (안 가요). Put **못** before it to say you can't (못 가요).
안 먹어요. (an meogeoyo.) = I don't eat.
일어나요 (wake up), 씻어요 (wash), 일해요 (work), 자요 (sleep). Time words such as 아침 (morning) and 밤 (night) take 에: 아침에.
Time words usually come near the start of the sentence.
Past tense: **-았어요 / -었어요 / -했어요**. Some verbs shorten: 가다 → 갔어요, 보다 → 봤어요.
Use **-(으)ㄹ 거예요** for plans: 가다 → 갈 거예요, 먹다 → 먹을 거예요.
내일 갈 거예요. (naeil gal geoyeyo.) = I will go tomorrow.
월요일 (Mon), 화요일 (Tue), 수요일 (Wed), 목요일 (Thu), 금요일 (Fri), 토요일 (Sat), 일요일 (Sun).
Months are a Sino-Korean number plus 월: 일월 (January), 삼월 (March), 오월 (May), 칠월 (July), 구월 (September), 십이월 (December).
Hours use native numbers plus 시: 한 시 (1:00), 두 시 (2:00), 세 시 (3:00), 열 시 (10:00). Ask 몇 시예요?
한 시 · 두 시 · 세 시 (han si · du si · se si)
매일 (every day), 자주 (often), 가끔 (sometimes), 항상 (always). Place them before the verb.
The past ending is -았/었어요: 했어요 (did), 왔어요 (came), 만났어요 (met), 샀어요 (bought), 잤어요 (slept).
생일 (birthday), 주말 (weekend), 선물 (gift). Ask 생일이 언제예요? and answer 제 생일은 오월이에요.
생일이 언제예요? (saengiri eonjeyeyo?) = When is your birthday?
Ask the price with 얼마예요? and ask for something with **… 주세요** (… please).
Ask **… 어디예요?** (Where is …?). Listen for 오른쪽 (right), 왼쪽 (left) and 직진 (straight).
화장실이 어디예요? (hwajangsiri eodiyeyo?) = Where is the restroom?
Add **-고 싶어요** to a verb stem to say what you want to do: 가다 → 가고 싶어요.
가고 싶어요. (gago sipeoyo.) = I want to go.
메뉴 (menu), 주문할게요 (I'll order), 물 더 주세요 (more water, please), 계산해 주세요 (the bill, please).
계산해 주세요. (gyesanhae juseyo.) = The bill, please.
버스 (bus), 지하철 (subway), 택시 (taxi), 기차 (train). Say how you go with -로/으로: 버스로 가요.
전화 (phone call), 전화번호 (phone number), 문자 (text message). 전화해요 means “I call”.
병원 (hospital), 약 (medicine), 아파요 (it hurts). Say the body part first: 머리가 아파요 (my head hurts).
-세요 and -아/어 주세요 make polite requests: 앉으세요 (please sit), 기다려 주세요 (please wait), 문을 열어 주세요 (please open the door).
같이 (together) invites someone: 같이 가요. 갈래요? asks “Do you want to go?” and 시간 있어요? asks “Do you have time?”
같이 가요. (gachi gayo.) = Let's go together.
In formal speech and at work, attach -ㅂ니다 to a verb or adjective stem that ends in a vowel and -습니다 to a stem that ends in a consonant. Questions end in -ㅂ니까 / -습니까.
저는 학생입니다. (jeoneun haksaengimnida.) = I am a student. / 이름이 무엇입니까? (ireumi mueosimnikka?) = What is your name?
The plain (written) style ends statements in -ㄴ다 / -는다 and past statements in -았다 / -었다. These forms are the base for reported speech in the next lessons.
나는 학교에 간다. (naneun hakgyoe ganda.) = I go to school. / 동생은 책을 읽는다. (dongsaengeun chaegeul ingneunda.) = My younger sibling reads a book.
A verb or adjective can describe a noun: -(으)ㄴ for adjectives and past actions, -는 for present actions, -(으)ㄹ for future or planned actions, placed before the noun.
저는 맛있는 음식을 좋아해요. (jeoneun masinneun eumsigeul joahaeyo.) = I like delicious food. / 예쁜 꽃을 샀어요. (yeppeun kkocheul sasseoyo.) = I bought pretty flowers.
Join two clauses with -아/어서 (reason or sequence), -지만 (contrast), -(으)니까 (reason), -(으)면 (if) and -(으)려고 (in order to).
피곤해서 일찍 잤어요. (pigonhaeseo iljjik jasseoyo.) = I was tired, so I went to bed early. / 비가 와서 집에 있었어요. (biga waseo jibe isseosseoyo.) = It rained, so I stayed home.
-(으)ㄹ 수 있다/없다 expresses ability or possibility, -아/어야 하다 obligation, and -아/어도 되다 permission.
저는 수영할 수 있어요. (jeoneun suyeonghal su isseoyo.) = I can swim. / 저는 한국어로 이야기할 수 있어요. (jeoneun hangugeoro iyagihal su isseoyo.) = I can talk in Korean.
Report what someone says or said: verb/adj + -다고 하다.
친구가 온다고 해요. (chinguga ondago haeyo.) = friend said coming
어디 가냐고 물었어요. (eodi ganyago mureosseoyo.) = asked where going
Report an imperative (-라고 하다) or propositive (-자고 하다).
빨리 오라고 했어요. (ppalli orago haesseoyo.) = told to come fast / 같이 가자고 했어요. (gachi gajago haesseoyo.) = suggested go together
Negative cause or delay (-느라고) and contrast despite circumstances (-는데도).
공부하느라고 바빴어요. (gongbuhaneurago bapasseoyo.) = busy studying / 비가 오는데도 갔어요. (biga oneundedo gasseoyo.) = went despite rain
The more... the more (-을수록) and natural inevitability (-기 마련이다).
만날수록 좋아요. (mannalsurok joayo.) = better as we meet / 사람은 실수하기 마련이에요. (sarameun silsuhagi maryeonieyo.) = bound to make mistakes
Looks like (-아/어 보이다) and appears to be (-는 모양이다).
행복해 보여요. (haengbokae boyeoyo.) = looks happy / 비가 오는 모양이에요. (biga oneun moyangieyo.) = seems raining
Pretend to do or be something: -(으)ㄴ/는 척하다.
아는 척해요. (aneun cheokaeyo.) = pretends to know
Express regret: 'I should have done...' -(으)ㄹ 걸 그랬어요.
일찍 올 걸 그랬어요. (iljjik ol geol geuraesseoyo.) = should have come early
Review indirect speech, complex connectors and nuanced expressions.
친구가 온다고 했어요. (chinguga ondago haesseoyo.) = friend said coming / 같이 밥 먹자고 했어요. (gachi bap meokjago haesseoyo.) = suggested eat together
Special honorific nouns and verbs for revered people: 진지, 주무시다, 편찮으시다.
할머니께서 진지를 드세요. (halmeonikkeseo jinjireul deuseyo.) = grandmother eats meal
Humble/honorific verbs when the action is directed toward an elder: 드리다, 뵙다, 여쭙다.
선물을 드려요. (seonmureul deuryeoyo.) = give gift honorific / 내일 봬요. (naeil bwaeyo.) = see tomorrow honorific
Passive verbs formed by adding -이/히/리/기-: 보이다, 들리다, 열리다, 닫히다.
문이 열려요. (muni yeollyeoyo.) = door opens / 창문이 닫혀요. (changmuni dachyeoyo.) = window closes
Verbs taking spontaneous or resulting passive forms: -아/어지다, -게 되다.
글씨가 써져요. (geulssiga sseojyeoyo.) = letter written well / 알게 되었어요. (alge doeeosseoyo.) = came to know
Causative verbs that make someone do an action: 보여 주다, 먹이다, 입히다.
사진을 보여 줘요. (sajineul boyeo jwoyo.) = shows photo / 아기에게 밥을 먹여요. (agiege babeul meogyeoyo.) = feeds baby
Make or cause someone to do something: -게 하다.
웃게 해요. (utge haeyo.) = makes laugh / 기다리게 했어요. (gidarige haesseoyo.) = made wait
High formal deferential style for announcements and ceremonies: -하십시오, -하십시다.
자리에 앉으십시오. (jarie anjeusipsio.) = please be seated / 출발하십시다. (chulbalhasipsida.) = let us depart
Polite speech using humble pronouns and verbs: 저희, 말씀 올리다.
인사 말씀 올립니다. (insa malsseum ollimnida.) = offer greeting words / 저희 학교입니다. (jeohui hakgyoimnida.) = our school humble
Review honorifics, passive, causative and formal polite registers.
할머니께 선물을 드렸어요. (halmeonikke seonmureul deuryeosseoyo.) = gave gift to grandmother / 문이 저절로 닫혔어요. (muni jeojeollo dachyeosseoyo.) = door closed by itself
Formal business email conventions: -에 관하여, 검토 부탁드립니다.
회의 안건에 관하여 말씀드립니다. (hoeui angeone gwanhayeo malsseumdeurimnida.) = regarding meeting agenda
Handling calls and messages: 통화 가능하신지요, 연결해 드리겠습니다.
지금 통화 가능하신지요? (jigeum tonghwa ganeunghasinjiyo?) = available to speak now / 담당자를 연결해 드리겠습니다. (damdangjareul yeongyeolhae deurigetseumnida.) = connecting person in charge
Proposing and changing appointment times: 변경하고자 합니다, 양해 부탁드립니다.
일정을 변경하고자 합니다. (iljeongeul byeongyeonghagoja hamnida.) = schedule change request / 너른 양해 부탁드립니다. (neoreun yanghae butakdeurimnida.) = ask kind understanding
Expressing views during meetings: 제 생각으로는, 찬성합니다, 추가 검토.
제 생각으로는 이번 안이 좋습니다. (je saenggakeoroneun ibeon ani jotseumnida.) = in my opinion proposal good / 적극 찬성합니다. (jeokgeuk chanseonghamnida.) = strongly agree
Giving status updates: 진행 상황을 보고합니다, 조치를 완료했습니다.
프로젝트 진행 상황을 보고합니다. (peurojekteu jinhaeng sanghwangeul bogohamnida.) = reporting project progress / 조치를 완료했습니다. (jochireul wallyohaesseumnida.) = completed action
Describing trends and numbers: 증가했습니다, 전년 대비.
매출이 증가했습니다. (maechuri jeunggahaesseumnida.) = sales increased / 전년 대비 상승했습니다. (jeonnyeon daebi sangseunghaesseumnida.) = increased compared to last year
Professional collaboration: 상호 협력을 희망합니다, 절충안 제시.
상호 협력을 희망합니다. (sangho hyeomnyeogeul huimanghamnida.) = hope mutual cooperation / 절충안을 제안합니다. (jeolchuganeul jeanhamnida.) = propose compromise
Exchanging cards and titles: 처음 뵙겠습니다, 명함 드립니다.
처음 뵙겠습니다, 명함 드립니다. (cheoeum boepgetseumnida, myeongham deurimnida.) = pleased to meet card / 김 부장님입니다. (gim bujangnimimnida.) = department manager kim
Review professional communications, formal correspondence and meetings.
안건을 검토해 주시기 바랍니다. (angeoneul geomtohae jusigi baramnida.) = please review agenda / 회의에서 뵙겠습니다. (hoeuieseo boepgetseumnida.) = see you at meeting
News headlines and compressed noun phrases: 물가 안정 대책 발표.
물가 안정 대책을 발표했습니다. (mulga anjeong daechaegeul balpyohaesseumnida.) = announced price measures
Reading short news articles: 친환경 에너지가 주목받고 있습니다.
친환경 에너지가 주목받고 있습니다. (chinhwan-gyeong eneojiga jumokbatgo isseumnida.) = clean energy popular
Common idioms with body parts: 발이 넓다 (wide network), 눈이 높다 (high standards).
김 대리는 발이 넓어요. (gim daerineun bari neobeoyo.) = has wide connections / 눈이 높아요. (nuni nopayo.) = high standards choose
Expressions for common situations: 바가지를 쓰다 (ripped off), 어깨가 무겁다 (heavy duty).
바가지를 썼어요. (bagajireul sseosseoyo.) = ripped off price / 어깨가 무거워요. (eokkaega mugeowoyo.) = heavy responsibility burden
Wisdom in proverbs: 소 잃고 외양간 고친다, 쇠뿔도 단김에 빼라.
